show: the stone of the stair well's lower walls is beaded with damp, though nothing has wet it
the old outer wall beside the great doors is beaded with damp, a cold sweat on the stone, and the flags under it are dull
the great oak doors have swollen in their frames: they drag on the flags and open with a longer creak than usual
the swifts and martins skim low over the lawn, near enough to the grass to brush it
the rooks and jackdaws keep to the trees along the lawn's edge, and a robin sits close by on the nearest sill
the rooks and jackdaws keep to the trees along the lawn's edge, and a robin sits close by on the nearest sill
from the head of a cold flue a pair of jackdaws call back and forth, chack, chack, and fall quiet when he comes near
under the greenhouse staging, among last season's leaves, something small and spiny snuffles about and goes on snuffling, not minding him at all
under the greenhouse staging a heap of leaves rises and falls, slowly, with something curled asleep in it

a small bat has come in at an open loop and flutters up and down under the roof of the passage, round and round, as if looking for the way out
far down the valley a long string of lit windows slides along beside the water, with a smudge of steam over it, and goes on out of sight
far down the valley a long plume of steam stands over the line, and the train beneath it draws away and is gone

down the well the lamps are being lit, gallery by gallery, the high ones already burning and the ones below him still dark, a flame at a time
on every gallery down the well the lamps burn steady
the lamps down the well burn low, and only a few are left alight on each gallery
Mr. Grimbleton goes slowly down the galleries with a taper, lighting the lamps the dusk has not reached, and grumbling at each
Mr. Grimbleton goes slowly down the galleries with a taper on a long pole, putting out a lamp here and there, and grumbling at each
